sources.name: van den Hoek et al. (2024), Normative data for the squat, bench press and deadlift exercises in powerlifting: Data from 809,986 competition entries. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 27(10):734-742
sources.measures: Best successful competition bench press divided by the lifter's bodyweight at that competition (ratio), from drug-tested, unequipped (raw) powerlifting meets in 15 federations worldwide, 1968-2022, lifters aged 12+; athletes can appear more than once. Deciles for males aged 18-35 (UN young adult band), N = 306,061 bench press entries. Also stratified by IPF weight class (Table 6) and by other age bands (Table 4).
sources.unit_as_published: multiple of bodyweight (kg lifted / kg bodyweight)
sources.notes: Mean and SD are for all 571,650 male entries (all ages), not just 18-35; male mean bodyweight 88.3 kg (SD 20.0). Paper publishes only the 10th to 90th deciles; no 95th or 99th percentile and no absolute-kg bench values in the main text (absolute totals are in supplementary Tables S4-S5, not the bench press alone). Other male age bands, p50/p90: 12-17 1.24/1.63 (N 69,494); 36-59 1.51/1.92 (N 111,152); 60-79 1.23/1.60 (N 22,289); 80+ 0.93/1.31 (N 789). Weight-class p90 bench ratios: 74 kg 2.00, 83 kg 1.96, 93 kg 1.89, 105 kg 1.82, 120 kg 1.75. Open access (CC BY 4.0); full text read from the UniSC repository copy.

sources.name: Strength Level, Bench Press Standards for Men and Women (kg)
sources.measures: Estimated one-rep-max bench press from sets logged by Strength Level app/site users (self-reported gym lifts, not competition), converted to an estimated 1RM; standards built from regression on the community data, with unrealistic lifts and automated entries excluded. Levels are defined as percentiles: Beginner = stronger than 5% of lifters, Novice 20%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 80%, Elite 95%. Values below are the male overall (all bodyweights) standards; the page also tabulates by bodyweight and by age.
sources.notes: n is the number of qualifying male results (9,906,475 of 10,923,537 qualifying results drawn from 48,718,584 community lifts, data 22 March 2015 to 10 March 2026); it counts lifts, not unique lifters. No 99th percentile is published. By age the male Elite (p95) value is 156 kg at 20, 160 kg at 25-40, 142 kg at 50, 120 kg at 60. By bodyweight the male Elite value is 136 kg at 70 kg, 151 kg at 80 kg, 165 kg at 90 kg, 179 kg at 100 kg. Self-selected, self-reported sample of people who log workouts; not the general population.

sources.name: Fitness Volt, Bench Press Standards by Bodyweight (competition percentiles by weight class)
sources.measures: Percentiles of best raw (unequipped) competition bench press for male lifters, computed by Fitness Volt from the OpenPowerlifting open dataset, segmented by bodyweight class. Tested and untested meets pooled; no year range stated. Values below are the 83 kg class (largest single class, n = 96,625 results).
sources.unit_as_published: lb with kg equivalents (kg shown here)
sources.notes: Only source found that publishes a 99th percentile, but only per weight class, never for all men combined. p99 in kg by class: 59 kg 162.5; 66 kg 160.5; 74 kg 172.5; 83 kg 187.5; 93 kg 200.0; 105 kg 215.0; 120 kg 230.0; 120+ not listed (125 kg class 250.0; 140 kg class 270.0). p50 by class: 74 kg 112.5; 93 kg 132.5; 105 kg 145.0; 120 kg 155.0. Not independent of van den Hoek 2024 (same underlying OpenPowerlifting records, but with different filters: Fitness Volt does not restrict to drug-tested federations). Commercial site; year is the access year, the page states no data cutoff.

sources.name: Strength Origins, Bench Press Standards (2025 competition percentiles)
sources.measures: Best competition bench press for male lifters in raw, drug-tested, full-power (squat-bench-deadlift) sanctioned meets held 1 Jan to 20 Dec 2025, ages 16-65, one best result per lifter per year; percentiles computed by Strength Origins from OpenPowerlifting. Overall (all bodyweights) men.
sources.unit_as_published: lb with kg equivalents (kg shown here)
sources.notes: n is unique male lifters. Page says it holds all 99 percentile values but displays only 10th to 90th; no p95/p99 shown. Not independent of van den Hoek 2024 or Fitness Volt (same OpenPowerlifting source). The Stronger app page (strongermobileapp.com/standards/bench-press), also OpenPowerlifting-derived, gives an all-bodyweight male median of 127 kg from 1,668,369 results / 556,880 lifters (tested men 125 kg vs untested 138 kg) but no upper percentiles.

definition: Best successful competition bench press divided by the lifter's bodyweight at that competition (ratio), from drug-tested, unequipped (raw) powerlifting meets in 15 federations worldwide, 1968-2022, lifters aged 12+; athletes can appear more than once. Deciles for males aged 18-35 (UN young adult band), N = 306,061 bench press entries. Also stratified by IPF weight class (Table 6) and by other age bands (Table 4).
caveat: No source publishes a 99th percentile for men's bench press across all bodyweights. The best peer-reviewed source (van den Hoek 2024) stops at the 90th decile and reports strength as a multiple of bodyweight, not kg; its 18-35 male p90 is 1.96x bodyweight. Strength Level gives kg but its top published level is the 95th percentile (160 kg for men overall, 2015-2026 self-reported app lifts). The only p99 figures (Fitness Volt, OpenPowerlifting-derived) exist per weight class only: 187.5 kg at 83 kg, 200 kg at 93 kg, 215 kg at 105 kg. Every competition-based source (van den Hoek, Fitness Volt, Strength Origins, Stronger) draws on the same OpenPowerlifting database and describes competitive powerlifters, a far stronger group than men in general; the Cooper Institute norms are closer to a general tested population but top out at the 95th percentile and are bodyweight ratios of uncertain vintage (2007 edition). The question asks about 'men' without qualification; all answers here are gated by either competing in powerlifting or logging lifts in an app.

new_metric.label: Bench press one-rep max
new_metric.definition: Heaviest weight a person can bench press for a single repetition, in kilograms; competition sources use the best successful raw (unequipped) lift at a sanctioned powerlifting meet, app sources use an estimated one-rep max from logged sets.
phrasings: how much can the top 1% of men bench press
how much should i be able to bench press

sources.name: FIDE / Jeff Sonas, 'Sonas Proposal: Repairing the FIDE Standard Elo rating system' (published on fide.com, 20 July 2023)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard (classical) Elo rating of every player on the FIDE rating list, active and inactive, grouped in 100-point bands; January 2023 list (405,074 players) and April 2023 list (approx. 414,000 players)
sources.notes: Published statements: 'the fact remains that 99% of rated players have ratings below 2400 Elo' and 'All players rated below 2000 Elo, which is the bottom 85% of rated players'. January 2023 band counts as published: 1000-1099 23,381; 1100-1199 30,475; 1200-1299 32,444; 1300-1399 33,844; 1400-1499 35,462; 1500-1599 37,324; 1600-1699 38,464; 1700-1799 37,749; 1800-1899 35,851; 1900-1999 31,844; 2000-2099 28,115; 2100-2199 19,818; 2200-2299 11,716; 2300-2399 5,518; 2400+ 3,069 (total 405,074). April 2023: 2300-2399 5,500; 2400+ 3,080; 'same 346,000 players below 2000' and '68,000 players' at 2000+. So 2400+ is about 0.76% of the list and 2300+ about 2.1%; the exact top-1% cutoff sits inside the 2300-2399 band. Pre-dates the March 2024 FIDE compression, which raised all sub-2000 ratings (minimum now 1400) but left ratings of 2000+ unchanged, so the top-1% cutoff is unaffected by it. Document is by FIDE's rating consultant and hosted by FIDE; no mean or SD given.

sources.name: FIDE October 2026 standard rating list, tabulated by JD Chess (research data file elo-2026-10-03.json)
sources.measures: FIDE Standard rating of every player on the October 2026 standard list with a positive published rating and no inactive flag (per-rating counts from the official standard_rating_list_xml.zip, archive dated 2 October 2026, SHA-256 recorded)
sources.notes: Median 1700 is stated in the file. The p99 value is NOT stated: the file gives per-rating counts, from which 2,728 active players are rated 2350 or above and 1,710 are 2400 or above (2300+: 4,136; 2200+: 8,324; 2000+: 27,857). One percent of 221,400 is 2,214, so the top-1% cutoff lies between 2350 and 2400; 2375 is the midpoint of that interval, not a published figure. The accompanying blog page publishes shares at or above thresholds: 2300 = 1.9%, 2400 = 0.8% of active published players. Active-only pool (inactive-flagged players excluded), minimum rating 1400 since the 2024 compression. Third-party tabulation with transparent method; treat as a cross-check on the FIDE/Sonas figure rather than an independent source.

sources.name: Lichess weekly rating distribution pages (rapid and blitz), histogram data captured 3 October 2026 in the JD Chess data file
sources.measures: Lichess Glicko-2 rating of players shown in the weekly rapid and blitz rating-distribution histograms (players with recent activity; 25-point bins from 400 to 2824); rapid n = 504,630, blitz n = 703,048
sources.notes: Rapid: median bin 1375-1399 (p50 given as bin midpoint); summing published bucket counts from the top, 5,040 players are rated 2250 or above against a top-1% size of 5,046, so the rapid top-1% cutoff is about 2250 (located from bucket counts, not stated by Lichess). Blitz (n = 703,048): median bin 1475-1499; 6,337 players at 2400+ and 7,412 at 2375+ against a top-1% size of 7,030, so the blitz top-1% cutoff is about 2375-2400. Classical page shows 41,171 players this week but its histogram was not captured. Lichess ratings are on a different scale from FIDE and the pool is online players active that week, not federation-rated players.

sources.name: US Chess Federation, USCF Regular Rating Distribution Chart as of November 1, 2004
sources.measures: US Chess regular (over-the-board) rating of all rated members, with cumulative percentile per 100-point band, split into all members, non-scholastic and scholastic
sources.notes: Published cumulative percentiles: through 2100-2199 = 98.13%, through 2200-2299 = 99.19% (all members), so the 99th percentile falls in the 2200-2299 band; p99 reported as the band floor. Non-scholastic (n = 49,458, average 1198): through 2200-2299 = 98.93%, through 2300-2399 = 99.39%, so p99 is in the 2300-2399 band. Scholastic (n = 15,997, average 668). Average rating 1068 for all members. Dated 2004 and flagged by US Chess as possibly no longer current; a national (US) pool that includes many scholastic players, so not comparable to the FIDE world list. US Chess Ratings Committee reports for 2025 and 2026 (glicko.net) discuss distribution trends but publish no percentile table.

definition: FIDE Standard (classical) Elo rating of every player on the FIDE rating list, active and inactive, grouped in 100-point bands; January 2023 list (405,074 players) and April 2023 list (approx. 414,000 players)
caveat: 'Rated players' is ambiguous. The primary answer uses the FIDE standard (over-the-board classical) list, where FIDE's own 2023 analysis states 99% of rated players are below 2400 and the October 2026 active list places the cutoff between 2350 and 2400 (roughly FIDE Master level). That pool is gated: FIDE publishes no rating below 1400 (1000 before March 2024), so it excludes most casual and club players. National federation pools give lower cutoffs (US Chess all members, 2004: 2200-2299 band). Online pools are on different scales: Lichess rapid top 1% is about 2250 and blitz about 2375-2400 among players active that week; chess.com publishes no distribution table. FIDE ratings deflated through the 2010s and were compressed in March 2024, which changed the bottom of the list but not ratings above 2000. No source states an exact top-1% rating; the FIDE figure is a band, and the Lichess and 2026 FIDE cutoffs were located from published counts rather than quoted.

new_metric.label: FIDE chess rating (standard)
new_metric.definition: A player's FIDE Standard (classical time control) Elo rating as published on the monthly FIDE rating list, among all players holding a published rating.
phrasings: what chess rating is the top 1%
what elo is top 1 percent of chess players
how good is a 2000 chess rating
what chess rating puts you in the top 1 percent
average chess rating of rated players

sources.name: Intertel, Join us: qualifying scores (99th percentile)
sources.measures: Minimum composite score on supervised intelligence tests that Intertel accepts as evidence of a score at or above the 99th percentile; Wechsler Full Scale IQ (WISC, WAIS, WPPSI), Stanford-Binet 5 IQ, Cattell scales. Stated criterion: 'The only criterion for membership is a score at or above the 99th percentile level on a qualifying and valid supervised test of intelligence.'
sources.unit_as_published: IQ points (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 for Wechsler and SB5)
sources.notes: Wechsler FSIQ 135; Stanford-Binet 5 IQ 135; Cattell Culture Fair IQ 140 and Cattell B / Cattell Verbal IQ 156 (SD 16 and SD 24 scales); California Test of Mental Maturity 137; Otis-Lennon 138. Intertel uses the composite score, not subtests, and does not accept the abbreviated WASI. The page's metadata dates it to about 2020; the live site redirected on fetch, values come from the search index of the same URL.

sources.name: Pearson, WAIS-IV sample Score Report (composite score to percentile rank)
sources.measures: Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, Fourth Edition composite scores (mean 100, SD 15) with the percentile rank Pearson's norm tables assign to each, for one illustrative examinee aged 70. Percentile ranks are relative to same-age peers in the US standardization sample (2,200 adults aged 16 to 90, norms published 2008).
sources.unit_as_published: composite standard score (IQ points) and percentile rank
sources.notes: Points read from the sample report's Composite Score Summary: PSI 122 = PR 93, PRI 123 = PR 94, WMI 133 = PR 99, FSIQ 139 = PR 99.5, VCI 145 = PR 99.9, all labelled 'Very Superior' at 130+. Not a full percentile table; it shows Pearson's own mapping at a few scores and confirms that 133 already rounds to the 99th percentile rank. The full table is in the WAIS-IV Technical and Interpretive Manual, which is not freely available.

sources.name: Triple Nine Society, Qualifying test scores (99.9th percentile)
sources.measures: Minimum scores the society accepts as evidence of the 99.9th percentile: WAIS Full Scale IQ, WISC Full Scale IQ (ages 15 to 16), Stanford-Binet 5 (age 16+), earlier Stanford-Binet forms, Cattell, RAIT.
sources.unit_as_published: IQ points (deviation IQ, mean 100, SD 15 for Wechsler and SB5)
sources.notes: WAIS FSIQ 146; WISC FSIQ 146; SB-5 146; SB Form L/M 151 and SB-IV 149 (SD 16 scales); Cattell IIIB 173 (SD 24); HAWIE-R 146; RAIT 146. WAIS-III not accepted for test dates after 15 February 2015 because of norm ageing. The page itself does not print the percentile; the 99.9th percentile criterion is the society's constitution.

definition: Minimum composite score on supervised intelligence tests that Intertel accepts as evidence of a score at or above the 99th percentile; Wechsler Full Scale IQ (WISC, WAIS, WPPSI), Stanford-Binet 5 IQ, Cattell scales. Stated criterion: 'The only criterion for membership is a score at or above the 99th percentile level on a qualifying and valid supervised test of intelligence.'
caveat: IQ is a norm-referenced score, so the percentile is built into the scale rather than measured in a population survey: Wechsler (WAIS-5, WAIS-IV, WISC-V) and Stanford-Binet 5 composites are scaled to mean 100, SD 15 against a US standardization sample (WAIS-IV n=2,200 adults aged 16 to 90, norms 2008; WAIS-5 n=2,020, norms 2024; WISC-V n=2,200 children, 2014), and 135 is the score those publishers' tables place at the 99th percentile; a Pearson sample report shows 133 already rounding to percentile rank 99 and 139 at 99.5. Percentile ranks are relative to same-age peers in that sample, not to the world population, and the mapping only holds on an SD-15 scale: older Stanford-Binet forms (SD 16) and Cattell scales (SD 24) put the 99th percentile at about 137 and 140 or 156 respectively. Scores on tests with old norms drift upward over time (Flynn effect), so high-IQ societies reject results from superseded editions. The 99th-percentile value comes from society admission thresholds that quote the publishers' norms, not from an independent empirical distribution; a full publisher percentile table is only in the paid technical manuals.

new_metric.label: IQ score
new_metric.base_noun: people who take a standardised IQ test
new_metric.definition: Full-scale score on a supervised, individually administered intelligence test such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale or Stanford-Binet 5, scaled to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 against the test's same-age standardization sample.
phrasings: what IQ score is the top 1%
what IQ do you need to be in the top 1 percent
how rare is an IQ of 140
what IQ do you need for Mensa

sources.name: US Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine, Technical Report T94-7: Army Physical Fitness Test (APFT): Normative Data on 6022 Soldiers (Knapik et al., 1994; data from the 1988 Active Army Physical Fitness Survey)
sources.measures: Number of correct push-ups completed in 2 minutes on the APFT; 5,346 male and 676 female soldiers at 14 US installations, age-banded as the APFT standards are. Percentile tables run from the 1st to the 99th percentile per age band.
sources.notes: Values above are Table 5, males 22-26 years (n=1688, the largest band). Other male bands (Tables 4, 6-9), read from the scanned PDF at archive.org (DTIC mirror ADA274547 returned 403): 17-21 (n=1157) p50 52, p90 70, p95 74, p99 83, mean 53.1, SD 11.6; 27-31 (n=1017) p50 49, p90 69, p95 76, p99 82, mean 50.7, SD 12.7; 32-36 (n=825) p50 46, p90 65, p95 73, p99 84, mean 47.4, SD 13.1; 37-41 (n=382) p50 41, p90 62, p95 70, p99 80, mean 44.2, SD 12.4; 42-46 (n=217) p90 53, p95 61, p99 70, mean 38.4, SD 11.5 (p50 for 42-46 came from OCR text and was out of sequence, so it is not reported). Table 3, all male soldiers regardless of age: mean 50.4, SD 13.0 (no all-age percentiles are given). Bands 27-31 to 42-46 were taken from the archive.org OCR text, Tables 4-5 from the page images. Sample is serving soldiers who must pass the APFT, so it is fitter and younger than the general male population; the 2-minute limit means counts are higher than one-minute or untimed-to-failure protocols.

sources.name: Cooper Institute fitness norms (one-minute push-ups) as reproduced in McKenzie County Sheriff's Office 'New Cooper Standards Age & Gender' table
sources.measures: Push-ups completed in one minute, males, percentile rows 5 to 99 by age decade (20-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60+). The sheriff's office reproduces Cooper Institute norms; the underlying Cooper publication (Physical Fitness Assessments and Norms for Adults and Law Enforcement) could not be opened directly, so the edition and sample size are unverified.
sources.notes: Values above are males 20-29. Other male bands: 30-39 p50 27, p90 46, p95 52, p99 86; 40-49 p50 21, p90 36, p95 40, p99 64; 50-59 p50 15, p90 30, p95 39, p99 51; 60+ p50 15, p90 26, p95 28, p99 39. Cooper norms come from Cooper Clinic patients and law-enforcement applicants, not a population sample; the p99 of 100 for 20-29 is a large jump from p95 (62) and may reflect a small tail. Document date is the reproduction date (March 2018), not the data year.

sources.name: Texas Department of Public Safety, Performance Standards for Males by Age (physical readiness test chart)
sources.measures: Push-ups with no time limit, percentile rows 1 to 99 for males in 5-year bands (20-24 to 50+). The chart does not state its data source or year and the rows rise in near-constant steps, so it reads as a constructed standards table rather than a published distribution.
sources.notes: Values above are males 20-24. p99 by band: 25-29 72; 30-34 68; 35-39 66; 40-44 63; 45-49 61; 50+ 59. p50 by band: 25-29 49; 30-34 47; 35-39 45; 40-44 43; 45-49 42; 50+ 40. Year is unknown; 2024 is the approximate fetch-era posting. Treat as low confidence because provenance is unstated.

sources.name: Kjær IGH, Torstveit MK, Kolle E, Hansen BH, Anderssen SA. Normative values for musculoskeletal- and neuromotor fitness in apparently healthy Norwegian adults. BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation 2016;8:37
sources.measures: Modified push-ups (with a hand-clap behind the back between reps) completed in 40 seconds, nationally sampled Norwegian adults aged 20-64.9, data 2008-2009; 342 men completed the test.
sources.notes: Only mean, SD and quartiles are published; no median or upper percentiles. Men 20-29.9 (n=39): mean 14.2, SD 3.2, Q1-Q3 12-16. Protocol is not comparable to a standard push-up count. Included to show that the only random population sample found uses a different test and gives no p99.

definition: Number of correct push-ups completed in 2 minutes on the APFT; 5,346 male and 676 female soldiers at 14 US installations, age-banded as the APFT standards are. Percentile tables run from the 1st to the 99th percentile per age band.
caveat: No national statistics office or population survey publishes a 99th percentile for standard push-ups. The only official source with a p99 is the US Army's 1988 APFT normative study (male soldiers, 2-minute test): about 83-84 push-ups for men under 37, falling to 70 at ages 42-46. Cooper Institute norms (1-minute test, clinic and law-enforcement clientele) give a p99 of 100 for men 20-29 and 86 for 30-39, but the Cooper tables were only reachable through a sheriff's office reproduction. Protocols differ (1 minute, 2 minutes, untimed, cadence-capped) and are not interchangeable, and every source is a gated or self-selected sample fitter than the general male population. If shipped, label the fact as 'US Army male soldiers, 2-minute test, 1988' rather than 'men'.

new_metric.label: Push-ups in one test
new_metric.definition: Number of correctly performed push-ups completed in a single test; the US Army APFT allows two minutes, Cooper Institute norms use one minute or no time limit.
phrasings: how many push ups can the top 1% of men do
how many pushups should i be able to do
average number of push ups for men
how many push ups is elite
